newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean chipmaker LG Semicon net profit plunges.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean chipmaker LG Semicon net profit plunges.

text.p: South Korean chip maker LG Semicon Co on Wednesday announced an 88 percent drop in 1996 net profit due to a freefall in memory chip prices and analysts said they saw no immediate end to the company's woes.

LG Semicon, one of South Korea's top three makers of dynamic random access memory (DRAM) chips and a unit of the LG Group, said after-tax net profit fell to 91.11 billion won ($105.7 million) from 778.49 billion won in 1995.
Sales fell to 2.1 trillion won in 1996 from 2.52 trillion a year earlier.
Bae Young-pyo, LG's executive director in charge of planning and finance, said the company's focus on production of higher value-added items rescued the bottom line.
"Last year's profit was attributable to our efforts to expand production of higher value-added items and reduce raw material costs," Bae told reporters.
Last year the unit price of 16-megabit DRAM chips, which are most widely installed in personal computers, fell about 80 percent due to a severe global oversupply.
Analysts said it was too early to say whether the recent recovery in 16-megabit DRAM prices would be sustained.
"Production cuts since late last year pushed up chip prices, but we are still cautious for the long term," said Tony Jung, an analyst at Jardine Fleming Securities.
The unit price of 16-megabit DRAM chips is now hovering at around $9-$9.5 in international spot markets, compared with around $6 at the end of 1996.

Last month LG Semicon announced it would shift away from producing 16-megabit chips. Samsung Electronics Co, the world's largest memory chip supplier, also said it would further control output of 16-megabit DRAM chips. "LG relies heavily on memory chip sales, and it's too early to say whether the strength of chip prices will hold and how much it will contribute to LG's annual earnings," said Jang Yun-yong, an analyst at Hyundai Securities.
LG Semicon depends on DRAM chips for nearly 90 percent of its sales, with the remainder coming from sales of non-memory chips such as application specific integrated circuits.
Analysts predicted Taiwanese makers would start massively supplying chips on world markets later this year.

"Taiwanese makers are a serious variable for this year's memory chip price trend because volumes from the country are expected to account for about 20 percent of the global market," said Jang of Hyundai.
